# Block 3: Context, disclosure and autonomy {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
```

Two questions decide how far you can trust an AI `r glossary("assistant")`:
what can it see, and what can it do? First you trace what reached the model
provider in Block 2. Then you hand an `r glossary("agent")` a routine change
and check it.

*⏱ ~30 minutes · Start on `main`, Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode.*

:::{#block3-files .callout-note collapse="true"}

**What each tool can see.** The routes are the same in every tool; what
travels along them is not. The biggest difference is your R session: Claude
Code cannot see it, and Posit Assistant works inside it.

| | Claude Code | Posit Assistant | Browser chat |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Route 1:** what you paste | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| **Route 2:** project files | Any file in the project, read without asking, unless a deny rule names it (habit 4, below) | Files in the project; it asks before reading outside it. `.Renviron` and `.env` are blocked | Only files you upload |
| **Route 3:** added by itself | `AGENTS.md`, the project folder, platform, date, git branch, uncommitted changes and recent commit messages | `AGENTS.md`, the R version, and the names and types of the objects in your session, not their values (this session context can be switched off) | Its memory or project files, if you have switched them on |
| **Route 4:** code it runs | `Rscript`, in a new R process that cannot see the objects in your console; it reads whatever the code prints | R code in your own live session, so the code can reach your objects; it reads whatever the code prints | None |
| Your console and plots | No | Yes: it can read your console history and view plots | Only what you paste |

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Context you hold in your head (instructor demonstration)

An assistant's answer about your data is only as good as its context. It is
reliable only when it has real information: something you pasted, a file it
read, or output from a command it ran. A data file supplies column names, but
not your question or your design.

**Where to run it:** a new browser chat (claude.ai or similar) with no project,
files or memory attached, such as a temporary chat. Not Claude Code: inside
the workshop repository it would read `AGENTS.md` and the data file (route 2),
so even the first prompt would get a specific answer.

Your instructor asks a new chat:

**Prompt (browser chat):**

```text
I have a dataset with pre and post measurements. How should I analyse it?
```

and then, in another new chat:

**Prompt (browser chat):**

```text
I have 72 voles, balanced across three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose,
High_dose) and two sexes (M, F). Each animal has body mass measured before
and after treatment, and a single post-treatment metabolic-rate reading.

My question is whether the high-dose treatment changes mass relative to
control, and whether the effect differs between sexes.

The dataset is small (n = 12 per cell). I will report effect sizes alongside
any inferential test. Given this design, what is a defensible primary
analysis, and what are the main threats to its validity?
```

The first gets a tour of options. The second can get a recommendation, because
the design now exists outside your head. Treat it as a proposal to check: the
primary analysis is your decision.

**Try it yourself** after the session: give each prompt to its own new browser
chat and compare the answers. For a third run, give the first prompt to Claude
Code in your workshop repository. It reads the data without being asked and
names the columns, but it still cannot know your question.
:::

::::{.callout-important}
## Working with confidential data: five habits, strongest first

An agent reads what it judges useful. If one route is closed, it often tries
another: refused a file, it may offer R code that opens the same file. So the
habits are listed from the one that always holds to the ones that only slow it
down.

1. **Keep it out of the project.** Put a synthetic or anonymised copy in the
   project, and run the final analysis on the real data yourself, outside the
   agent's folder. A file that is not there cannot be read by any route.
2. **Know your account.** Commercial accounts (Team, Enterprise, API) are not
   used for model training. On Pro or Max, set `/privacy-settings`. Check your
   institution's approval, ethics approval and data agreements first.
3. **Read every R command before you approve it.** In Manual mode, Claude Code
   asks before it runs `Rscript`. Look for file paths in the code, and say No
   to any that would open a file you want kept out. You will see an agent
   offer this route in [Block 7](11g-data-cleaning.qmd).
4. **Add a deny rule as well,** in `/permissions`, for example
   `Read(/data/confidential/**)`. It stops Claude Code's own file reads and
   simple commands such as `cat` and `head`. It does not stop R code that
   opens the file, or a search of the whole project such as `grep -r`, which
   runs without asking. Treat it as a speed bump, not a wall
   ([Block 5](11f-enforced-controls.qmd)).
5. **Describe, don't show.** `names()` and `dim()` describe the data without
   showing values. `summary()` prints real minima and maxima. `print()`,
   `glimpse()` and `str()` print actual rows.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How it works: tool notes

- **Claude Code:**
  - There is no `.claudeignore` file.
  - Read-only commands such as `cat`, `head`, `grep` and `ls` never ask, even
    in Manual mode.
  - On macOS, Linux and WSL2, the `/sandbox` command adds an operating-system
    block on reading paths you list (`sandbox.filesystem.denyRead`). That block
    applies to R code too. The sandbox is not available on native Windows.
- **Posit Assistant:**
  - It blocks `.Renviron` and `.env` by default.
  - Its session context, the names and types of your objects, can be switched
    off.
  - Code it runs in your live session can still print values.
  - Its documentation does not say whether a deny rule can name a folder, so
    test one before you rely on it.
:::
::::


## Exercise 2: What can it do?

The model is the same at every `r glossary("rung")` of the autonomy ladder.
What changes is what it may do without asking you, which in Claude Code is set
by its `r glossary("permission mode")`. Rung 3, act with approval, is where
routine work stays checkable:

- you start from a commit, so you can revert any change;
- you see every edit and command first;
- a test checks the result, whatever the agent reports.

:::{.callout-note}
## The autonomy ladder

An assistant that advises leaves you to filter every change. An agent that acts
removes that filter, unless you put it back. The rungs differ in how much of
that filtering is left to you.

Each rung answers two questions: can the assistant change your files or run
code, and what do you approve?

| Rung | Changes files or runs code? | What you approve | Claude Code | Posit Assistant |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0. Suggest | No: it completes the line you are typing | Each suggestion, by accepting it | — | Next Edit Suggestions |
| 1. Ask | No: it answers in the chat | Nothing; it may still read files | — (no ask mode; Block 2's answer-only line is a request) | Ask mode (`/ask`) |
| 2. Plan | No edits: it proposes steps | The plan, before anything changes | `/plan` | `/plan` |
| 3. Act, with approval | Yes | Every edit and every command, except read-only ones | Manual (`default`): the workshop's starting mode | Normal mode |
| 4. Act, partly unsupervised | Yes | Only actions outside a set it may take alone | `acceptEdits` (edits and file commands); `auto` (a classifier approves actions) | Auto mode (`/auto`) |
| 5. Act, unsupervised | Yes | Nothing | `bypassPermissions` | YOLO mode (`/yolo`) |

In Claude Code, reading a project file never needs approval, at any rung.
From rung 3 up, what changes is which `r glossary("tool call", "tool calls")`
run without your approval. [Block 6](11k-build-an-agent.qmd), after lunch,
builds that approval step in code. Your workshop repository starts Claude Code
in **Manual**, although recent versions of Claude Code start in `auto`. Keep
Manual for confidential data. `/plan` may run commands to explore, and on
recent versions some run without asking you. Use only rungs 0 to 3 today. The
[quick reference](11-AI-programming-integrated.qmd#cc-quick-reference) lists
the commands for the other modes.

Each rung up removes a moment when you would have seen the action. In
`acceptEdits`, for example, file commands such as `cp` and `mv` run without
asking, so a `cp` over a raw data file needs no approval. The higher the rung,
the more an agent acts on its guesses about your conventions. That is why
[Block 4](11e-instructions-skills.qmd) writes them down.
:::

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Ask, plan, act (15 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Goal:** have the agent add a column and a plot script at rung 3, then check
its work with the diff and the tests, so that you trust the change because you
checked it, not because the agent reported it.

**Start state:** your workshop repository on `main`, Git pane clean, Claude
Code in Manual mode. Check its work from the R console and the Git pane
([checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work)).

**1. Plan (rung 2).** In Claude Code, type `/clear`, then:

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
/plan In scripts/explore_voles.R, add a mass_change_g column (mass_post_g
minus mass_pre_g) to the voles data frame itself. Create a new script
scripts/explore_mass_change_plot.R that plots mass_change_g by
treatment_arm and saves the figure to outputs/ with ggsave(). Don't run
anything; I'll check the scripts myself.
```

Before you approve, check that the plan names both files, adds the column to
`voles` itself, leaves `data/raw/` alone and saves the figure to `outputs/`. If
anything is missing, choose **No, keep planning** and say what to change.

**2. Act, with approval (rung 3).** Choose **Yes, manually approve edits**. It
is not the first option: the first, *Yes, and use auto mode* (or *Yes,
auto-accept edits*), switches the approvals off. Then read each edit before
you approve it. **Answer each request with plain Yes or No.** Never choose an
option that says *don't ask again*: it saves a rule that skips the question
from then on.

If it asks to run `git status` before it edits (`AGENTS.md` asks it to check),
answer Yes: that command only reads. It may also ask to run the new scripts
and the test suite with `Rscript`. Approve a run only if you can say what it
does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. For these, choose
**No**: you check the result yourself next.

**3. Read the diff.** Click **Diff** in the Git pane for each changed file.
Read it as you would a colleague's work: the diff shows every change, including
any you did not ask for.

**4. Record.** Start your `r glossary("AI-use log")`. The agent knows the
date, its model and what it did, so let it draft the line. Only you know what
you kept or changed, so that part stays yours.

**Prompt (Claude Code):**

```text
Create docs/ai-log.md and add one line for the work you just did, in the
form: date (YYYY-MM-DD); Claude Code (your model name); task; TODO.
Leave the last field as TODO.
```

Approve the new file after reading it. Then open it
(`usethis::edit_file("docs/ai-log.md")`) and replace `TODO` with what you kept
or changed. Check that the date and the model match what is shown above the
Claude Code prompt. The finished line looks like this:

```text
2026-10-19; Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5); added mass_change_g and a plot script; kept both after reading the diff
```

Writing it before you test means the tests check it too.

**5. Test, then commit.** Restart R (*Session → Restart R*) so that nothing
left in your session can make a test pass. Then run:

**In the R console:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))
```

`test_dir()` runs every `test*.R` file in `tests/`. The template ships them;
in this block, these are the ones that matter:

| File | Checks | Before this block |
|---|---|---|
| `test_explore.R` | `mass_change_g` in `voles` really is post minus pre; the plot script runs in a fresh R session and saves a figure in `outputs/` | Skipped: no plot script yet |
| `test_ai_log.R` | Every log line has four parts and a real date | Skipped: no log yet |
| `test_controls.R` | Manual mode, the deny rules and `AGENTS.md` are still in place ([Block 4](11e-instructions-skills.qmd)) | Already passing |

The other test files are for later blocks, and skip. Commit the log and both
scripts together (git ignores `outputs/`).

**Where tests like these come from in your own work.** None of these checks
needed the answer in advance. Each comes from what you asked for: the
definition of the column, a script that runs from a fresh session and saves a
file, a log line in the agreed form. So you can write them, or have the agent
draft them for you to read, *before* the agent does the work. They cannot tell
you whether the plot is a good one: you check that by looking.
[Block 8](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd) writes a test from scratch.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The test you just ran: `tests/test_explore.R`

```{r, eval = FALSE, file = here::here("_instructor", "template-files", "tests", "test_explore.R")}
```
:::

**You are done when** you have read every line of the diff, the tests show no
failures, the `explore` and `ai_log` lines of the test output show their tests
under **OK**, not **S** (skipped), and your first log line is committed with
both scripts.

**If it goes wrong:** select the unwanted change in the Git pane and click
**Revert**, then ask again more clearly. If `test_explore.R` says `voles` has
no `mass_change_g`, the agent made the column somewhere else: ask it to add the
column to `voles` itself. An **S** on `explore` or `ai_log` means its file is
missing or misnamed. Out of time? Carry on: at the end of Block 4,
`checkpoint-skills` holds this block's files (commit or discard your changes in
the Git pane first, so the switch is not blocked).

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stretch: reflect on the rungs

At which rung did you decide the most? Where would you have missed an unwanted
change without the diff?

**Payoff.** What did the agent do, how long did checking it take, and would you
automate this again?
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## At the command line

The same checks from a terminal (after `/exit`, or in a second Terminal tab):
`git status`, `git diff`, and `Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')"`.
:::

::::
:::

:::{#safe-recipe .callout-note}
## The safe vibe-coding recipe

1. **Commit**, so you start from a clean Git pane.
2. **Protect the inputs:** `/permissions` shows the deny rules, or you add one.
3. **Have the checks ready:** tests in `tests/` before the agent starts.
4. **Ask** in one prompt or skill, in Manual mode, reading each approval.
5. **Run the checks:** the test suite in a fresh R session.
6. **Read the diff** in the Git pane, then commit or revert.

You will use these six steps in Blocks 7 and 8. The template ships the
protections and the tests, so most of the work is checking that they are
there.
:::


:::{.callout-note}
## Check · Reproduce · Record

- **You can now:** hand an agent a routine multi-file change at rung 3,
  **trusted because** you read every diff and a test you did not write checks
  the result.
- **Check:** the Git pane's diff after every agent action; the agent's report
  that something "still runs" is a claim until a test confirms it.
- **Reproduce:** work only in a committed, clean repository, so every change
  is a diff you can inspect or revert.
- **Record:** your AI-use log starts here, in `docs/ai-log.md`.
:::


## Check your understanding

**You paste nothing, yet Claude Code names your columns correctly. How could it
know them?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "It cannot; it must be guessing",
  answer = "It read a file in your project or ran code that printed the data, and that output entered its context",
  "It can see every file on your computer",
  "It remembers your data from a previous conversation"
))`

**Your project's settings hold the deny rule `Read(/data/confidential/**)`.
Which of these can still read a file in that folder?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "Nothing: a deny rule blocks every route",
  "Only Claude Code's own Read tool",
  answer = "R code the agent runs with Rscript, or a search of the whole project such as grep -r, which runs without asking",
  "Only you, from the R console"
))`

**In Claude Code's acceptEdits mode, what does the agent do without asking?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "Nothing; acceptEdits only changes how diffs are displayed",
  "Only edits to files you have named",
  answer = "It edits files and runs common file commands such as cp and mv without asking, but still asks before other shell commands",
  "Everything, including all shell commands"
))`

**Which check still works whatever rung the agent ran at?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "The agent's own report that the task succeeded",
  "The approval prompts you saw while it worked",
  answer = "Reading the diff in the Git pane (or with git diff), and running the code or its tests yourself",
  "The plan the agent proposed before starting"
))`

## Access and cost

Plans and prices change; check before the session.

- **Claude Code** needs an Anthropic account, used through a subscription or an
  API key; see Anthropic's documentation for current options.
- **Posit Assistant** uses Posit AI Pass or your own provider key, including an
  Anthropic API key. In RStudio, providers are configured in the assistant's
  settings.
- **GitHub Copilot** bills in AI credits; check GitHub's plans page for what
  your plan includes.
- **Your institution** may have approved some of these tools and not others.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Trusting a repository's configuration

Project settings and hooks are code that runs on your machine. A cloned
repository can carry its own, so trust only repositories whose configuration
you have read.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## GitHub Copilot and the remote rung

Copilot offers the same ladder, plus a rung 6: its cloud agent works on your
repository on GitHub, on its own branch, and returns a pull request. The
self-study page [Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot's cloud agent](11l-copilot-cloud-agent.qmd) walks through it.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stretch: the same error at three levels of context

The code `voles |> mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post - mass_pre_g)` fails with
"object 'mass_post' not found". In three new browser chats, ask about it with
more context each time. First give the error message alone. Then give the
error plus the code. Last, give the error, the code and the output of
`glimpse(voles)`. With the code, a chat may guess `mass_post_g` by analogy
with `mass_pre_g`, but only the `glimpse()` output lets it confirm the name.
Column names you never supplied, or a famous dataset you never mentioned
(`penguins`, `mtcars`), are signs it is guessing.
:::
